summary: Suggests a mail mapping between X.400 (1988) or ISO 10021 messages and RFC 822 messages, for the Internet and UK Academic communities. It includes material lost in editing the previous edition. It is experimental and not a standard. It was replaced by RFC 1327 and RFC 2156.

eli5.summary: Two mail systems use different formats. This is a translation guide, fixed to put back parts that got lost.

questions: gateway between x.400 mail and internet mail
how does x.400 email map to internet email
subtitle: How to translate between two incompatible email systems at a gateway.

tldr.problem: X.400 (a formal international email standard) and RFC 822 (the internet email standard) were incompatible, yet both were deployed in different communities, requiring a translation mechanism between them.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1148 defines a complete mapping specification that translates between X.400 message structures and RFC 822 message formats, covering addresses, message headers, service indicators, and delivery notifications at a gateway.
tldr.outcome: This specification enabled the two email communities to interwork without requiring end systems to be modified, allowing messages to flow between X.400 and RFC 822 networks through translator gateways.

facts.label: Version
facts.value: Version 2 of X.400 mapping (first was RFC 987)

today: RFC 1148 is Experimental status and was superseded by RFC 1327 and RFC 2156. X.400 gateways are now rare as RFC 822/SMTP became dominant, but the mapping principles remain relevant for any protocol conversion.

sections.title: Two Email Systems That Needed to Talk
sections.content:
RFC 1148 solves a practical problem: making email work between two large, incompatible email systems. X.400 is the formal international standard for email, standardized by CCITT (now ITU) and ISO. RFC 822 is the Internet's email standard, used with protocols like SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol). Both had significant deployments in different communities, and they needed to exchange mail.

This RFC specifies how a gateway (a translator computer) can convert messages between the two formats so that an RFC 822 user in the Internet can send email to an X.400 user in an academic or government network, and vice versa. The challenge is that the two systems are fundamentally different in structure, terminology, and what services they support.

This is Version 2 of such a mapping, building on RFC 987. It updated that earlier specification to work with the full 1988 version of X.400 rather than the 1984 version, providing better support for X.400 communities adopting the newer standard.
sections.eli5: Two post office systems use completely different forms. A translator at the border changes one form into the other so people from both sides can mail each other.

sections.title: Understanding the Two Systems
sections.content:
RFC 822 defines email as simple text messages with a header and a body. The header consists of fields like From:, To:, Subject:, and Date:, all written in ASCII text. Messages are routed using domain names (like user@example.com) and rely on an underlying message transfer service (typically SMTP on the Internet) to deliver them.

X.400 is much more structured. It defines two main objects: an IPM (Interpersonal Message), which is the actual message, and an IPN (Interpersonal Notification), which is a receipt or notification. X.400 messages consist of headers (fields for subject, recipients, importance, and requested services) and a body that can contain multiple parts of different types (text, fax, file, etc.). Addresses in X.400 are structured as hierarchical attribute-value pairs, like a directory entry, rather than simple text addresses.

The RFC notes that both systems work above a message transfer layer. RFC 822 assumes an underlying 822-MTS service, while X.400 defines explicit MTS (Message Transfer System) and IPMS (Interpersonal Messaging System) layers.
sections.eli5: RFC 822 mail is like a postcard: simple text with basic address fields. X.400 mail is like a registered letter with many options, structured address components, and notification receipts.

sections.title: The Trickiest Problem: Addresses
sections.content:
RFC 1148 describes address mapping as the core challenge. RFC 822 addresses are simple strings like kille@ucl.ac.uk. X.400 O/R (Originator/Recipient) addresses are hierarchical structures with attributes such as Country (C), Administration Domain (ADMD), Organization (O), Organizational Unit (OU), Personal Name (PN), and others. An X.400 address might have 10 or more attribute-value pairs.

The RFC defines how to convert between them. For each X.400 attribute, a short key is assigned: C for Country, ADMD for Administration Domain, PN for Personal Name, and so on. These are combined into a slash-delimited string like /C=gb/ADMD=gold/O=ucl/OU=cs/CN=Kille/ which is closer to both systems. For personal names, the RFC defines a syntax like Marshall.Rose or M.T.Rose that is human-readable while remaining reversible.

The specification is designed to be reversible—applying the mapping twice should return you to the original—and to handle cases where messages traverse multiple gateways between the two systems. This prevents information loss or corruption in repeated translations.
sections.eli5: X.400 addresses have many parts: country, company, department, name. The gateway translates them to internet form and back without losing any information, so a reply can find the way home.

sections.title: Mapping Message Content and Services
sections.content:
Beyond addresses, the RFC maps all the other aspects of email. RFC 822 headers like From:, To:, Cc:, Subject:, Date:, and Message-ID: map directly to equivalent X.400 message heading fields. Some RFC 822 features are supported directly, like setting the message subject or specifying reply-to addresses. Others require extensions to RFC 822 or are stored as heading extensions (extra attributes) in X.400.

X.400 provides many services that RFC 822 does not: requesting delivery confirmation, setting message importance (urgent/normal/low), deferring delivery until a later time, specifying an expiry date, requesting a reply by a certain date, and others. The RFC shows how these are mapped into RFC 822, often as custom headers. For example, an X.400 message with importance="urgent" becomes an RFC 822 message with a Priority: urgent header.

The gateway must also handle X.400 notifications: when a message is delivered, failed, or read, X.400 systems send back Delivery Reports (successful or failed) or Interpersonal Notifications (read receipts). These are converted to RFC 822 format for transmission back across the gateway.
sections.eli5: The gateway translates special settings: urgent becomes a priority flag, read receipts become status emails, and unfamiliar options get stored as notes that the other side can ignore.

sections.title: Design Principles and Scope
sections.content:
The RFC outlines five design principles. First, the mapping should be pragmatic—no complex transformations just for academic purity. Second, subject to that, functionality across the gateway should be as high as possible. Third, information must not be discarded; if a feature cannot be fully mapped, the information is preserved as an extension rather than lost.

Fourth, the specification recognizes that gateways operate at a level above their conceptual layer: they must understand message semantics from the level above (IPMS/IPMS service) to perform meaningful translation. Fifth, mappings should be reversible to support repeated translation through multiple gateways.

The RFC explicitly states what it does NOT cover: it does not define extensions to RFC 822 to access all X.400 services (that would require modifying 822 systems), and it does not define X.400 user interface specifications. The goal is to enable interworking while preserving compatibility for existing systems on both sides.
sections.eli5: The translation tries to keep everything meaningful, not lose information, and work the same way even if you translate back and forth. It works for both systems without making anyone change their email software.

right.title: X.400 (International Standard)
